interview_metadata.name: Keng Dayrit
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Manila in 1976, but my family was already mixed in every way. My father was Filipino, from Pampanga, and my mother was Vietnamese; her family had come through the Philippines after the war. At home we had Tagalog, Vietnamese, and some English all mixed together, and food was the way everybody made peace after long days. My parents came to Queens in 1991, when I was fifteen, first staying with an aunt in Elmhurst and then moving toward Queens Village. I did not go far in school. I had finished about eighth grade back home, and after we came here I tried school for a little while, but my English was rough and my family needed money, so I started helping my father with building repairs, cleaning work, painting, plumbing, whatever people would pay cash for. I married my wife, Mai-Lan, who everyone calls Lani, in the late 1990s. We built our life around family, church holidays, Tet, Noche Buena, and doing things carefully with money. We have two children: Marielle, who is twenty-one and away at SUNY Albany most of the school year, and Nico, who is sixteen and still at home. I worked many years doing maintenance and handyman work, but I have not been in the regular workforce for a while now. These days I manage the house, volunteer at the senior center, cook, garden, help neighbors with small repairs when I can, and try to keep my anxiety from running the show.

follow_ups.question: What do you remember most clearly about arriving in Queens as a teenager?
follow_ups.response: The noise and the languages. On Jamaica Avenue and in Elmhurst I heard Spanish, Tagalog, Mandarin, Korean, everything, and I remember thinking I was lost but also not the only person who was lost.

follow_ups.question: Who was most important in helping you adjust then?
follow_ups.response: My mother, because she kept the house steady, and one Filipino uncle from church who would bring me along on repair jobs. He showed me how to talk to customers without being embarrassed.

follow_ups.question: What part of your early life still shows up in your life now?
follow_ups.response: Budgeting and cooking. When you come with little money, you learn exactly what is in the pantry, and you learn how to make one pot feed six people.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was leaving school for work after we came to New York. I wanted to stay in school because I liked drawing and photography, and a teacher told me I had a good eye. But at home rent was tight, my father was taking whatever repair jobs he could find, and my mother was doing sewing and kitchen work. I remember sitting at the kitchen table in Queens Village with bills spread out, and I knew if I worked with my father we could breathe a little. So I left school and became the helper. That choice gave me skills and pride, but it also left a hole in me. Even now, when I walk through a museum or help seniors write recipes down, I think, maybe that was the education I made for myself later.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone try to convince you to stay in school?
follow_ups.response: One teacher did, Mr. Hanley, from the high school program I briefly attended. He told me, 'Keng, you don't have to disappear,' and I still remember that.

follow_ups.question: How did your parents react to that choice?
follow_ups.response: They were grateful but also sad. My father said family survives together, but my mother kept telling me I could study again someday.

follow_ups.question: Do you think that decision shaped your current community work?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I know what it feels like to have no official paper saying you are smart, so I like teaching cooking in a way where older people and immigrants feel respected.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. The pressure was there already, but I did make the choice consciously. I remember choosing work clothes over a backpack.

follow_ups.question: Did it feel like you had real options?
follow_ups.response: A little, but not the kind of options people talk about when they have savings. My option was help now or watch my parents struggle harder.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about that choice today?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. I am proud I helped, but I still feel a small grief when forms ask for education.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes, if someone had helped with tutoring, translation, or even a small family assistance program, maybe I could have stayed in school longer. We did not know how to ask.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: A counselor who understood immigrant families and could explain night school or work-study clearly.

follow_ups.question: Did your family use any community organizations then?
follow_ups.response: Mostly church and relatives. We did not really know nonprofit services except food pantry once or twice.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: My wife Lani is the center person for me. She is Vietnamese Filipino too, but more Vietnamese on her mother's side, and she works as a home health aide. She is practical, not dramatic, and she has saved me many times from my own anxious spinning. Our daughter Marielle is twenty-one, studying sociology at SUNY Albany, and she is the one who pushes me to try new art exhibits or send in workshop proposals. Our son Nico is sixteen, in high school, quiet but funny, and he plays soccer and video games with his cousins. My mother, Corazon Bich, is seventy-six and lives with my sister in Flushing, but I see her usually twice a week. Family for us is not just the people under the roof; it is who shows up for soup, rides to appointments, and holidays.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal week with your immediate family look like?
follow_ups.response: Weeknights I cook around six, Nico comes home after practice or homework club, and Lani comes in tired around seven-thirty. Marielle calls on Sundays unless she is home from school.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Lani usually do together?
follow_ups.response: We grocery shop at H Mart or the Filipino store, watch Knicks games, and drink tea late at night after the kitchen is cleaned.

follow_ups.question: How do you stay connected with your daughter while she is away?
follow_ups.response: Text messages, family group chat, and Sunday video calls. I send her photos of food and she sends me pictures from campus.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have one younger sister, Teresa, in Flushing, and one older brother, Ramon, in Jersey City. We are close, but busy, so mostly we connect through family meals and helping with our mother.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see them?
follow_ups.response: Teresa about once or twice a week because of my mother. Ramon maybe once a month unless there is a birthday.

follow_ups.question: Who do you call first in a family emergency?
follow_ups.response: Usually Teresa, because she is organized and answers fast.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small but steady circle. My closest friend is Jun, who runs a little auto shop near Hollis; we have known each other since the 1990s. I also spend time with Luis and Ahmed from Saturday basketball in Astoria. At the senior center, there is Ms. Evelyn, a retired nurse, and Mr. Tran, who grows herbs like he is running a farm in a window box. Those people matter because they see different sides of me: the handyman, the cook, the anxious guy, the person trying to become useful in the community.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see friends outside family?
follow_ups.response: Basketball friends most Saturdays if my knees cooperate. Jun I see every couple weeks, usually coffee or helping each other with a small repair.

follow_ups.question: Do you have people you talk to when you're worried?
follow_ups.response: Lani first, then sometimes Jun. I don't always like admitting worry, but Jun understands without making a big speech.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: Queens Village is not fancy, but it is home. We have single-family houses, small yards, buses, people from the Caribbean, South Asia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Bangladesh, everywhere. On our block you smell curry one house, adobo another, barbecue another. I like that I can get to groceries, church, the senior center, and the train with some planning, though transit can be slow. I keep a little backyard garden with basil, mint, Thai basil, tomatoes, and sometimes bitter melon. The neighborhood feels like working families trying to hold things together.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend the most time nearby?
follow_ups.response: The backyard, the senior center kitchen, Cunningham Park when I need a walk, and the Asian groceries along Hillside or in Flushing when I make a bigger trip.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors know each other on your block?
follow_ups.response: Yes, not everyone deeply, but enough to borrow a ladder, watch a package, or send over food during holidays.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Mostly I feel safe. I am careful late at night, especially around bus stops, but on my block I know the faces and that helps.

follow_ups.question: Are there times you avoid going out?
follow_ups.response: After midnight I don't wander unless I have to pick someone up.

follow_ups.question: What makes you feel safer?
follow_ups.response: Porch lights, neighbors outside, and knowing who belongs on the block.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is community and food and familiar people. The downside is cost, traffic, noise, and sometimes feeling like the city forgets outer Queens until something breaks.

follow_ups.question: What city services affect you most?
follow_ups.response: Sanitation, buses, street repairs, and tree trimming. A bad sidewalk matters when my mother visits.

follow_ups.question: Have you thought about moving?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but our family roots are here and I don't want to start over.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my wife Lani, and our son Nico. Marielle is away at SUNY Albany during the semester, but her room is still her room and she comes home for breaks. No one else is staying here right now. My mother visits, but she lives with my sister in Flushing.

follow_ups.question: What are the usual household roles?
follow_ups.response: I cook, shop, fix things, and manage bills. Lani earns most of the money and handles medical appointments. Nico does trash, dishes, and yard cleanup when reminded.

follow_ups.question: Does Marielle keep belongings at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, books, winter clothes, and art supplies. When she is home the house feels louder in a good way.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone here is permanent, except Marielle is away at school part of the year.

follow_ups.question: Do you consider Marielle part of the household?
follow_ups.response: Yes, absolutely. She is away for school, not moved out fully.

follow_ups.question: Any short-term guests now?
follow_ups.response: No, no short-term guests right now.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes my nephew sleeps over after family gatherings, and my mother may stay one night if appointments run late.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two.

follow_ups.question: Where do they sleep when they stay?
follow_ups.response: Usually the sofa bed in the small den.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: Yes, my daughter Marielle is away at SUNY Albany during the school year.

follow_ups.question: When is she usually home?
follow_ups.response: Winter break, summer, some long weekends.

follow_ups.question: Is anyone away for medical reasons?
follow_ups.response: No, not for medical reasons.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday and Tuesday are usually house and errands: laundry, bills, groceries, and checking what needs repair. Wednesday I often go to the senior center to help prep lunch or plan a cooking activity. Thursday I may visit my mother in Flushing and bring her soup or drive her to an appointment. Friday is cleaning and cooking for the weekend. Saturday morning I try to play pickup basketball in Astoria, and Sunday is family, church some weeks, and a big meal. Evenings are when I experiment in the kitchen, listen to jazz, or edit photos.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wake up and go to bed?
follow_ups.response: I wake around 6:15, sometimes earlier if anxious. I try to sleep by 11, but bad nights become midnight snack nights.

follow_ups.question: Which day feels busiest?
follow_ups.response: Wednesday, because the senior center kitchen has its own rhythm and I have to be organized.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: Right now I do not have a paid job. I used to do building maintenance, handyman repairs, painting, basic plumbing, and small electrical fixes. Since leaving the regular workforce, I still do unpaid repairs at home and occasionally help relatives or seniors, but I don't count that as a job. My main scheduled commitment is volunteering at the senior center, usually one or two days a week. I am also trying to shape that into a real community cooking workshop someday.

follow_ups.question: When did you stop regular paid work?
follow_ups.response: Around 2021. My back, my knees, and anxiety were all getting worse, and Lani and I decided I should step back.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever take cash repair jobs now?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. If it is family, I usually don't charge. I avoid taking paid jobs because I don't want to overpromise with my body.

follow_ups.question: What does volunteering involve?
follow_ups.response: Chopping, setting up tables, translating simple instructions, teaching recipes, and checking in with seniors who seem lonely.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep the household budget every Sunday night. I write bills in a notebook and also keep a spreadsheet Marielle helped me make. I water the garden, check the basement for leaks, cook most dinners, and make sure Nico has what he needs for school. I also check on my mother by phone every morning because she gets nervous if no one calls.

follow_ups.question: What is your budgeting routine like?
follow_ups.response: Receipts in a shoebox first, then Sunday night I enter groceries, utilities, transportation, and medical costs.

follow_ups.question: What responsibilities feel most stressful?
follow_ups.response: Medical bills and anything with official forms. Forms make me feel like I am back being fifteen and confused.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Recently I added more structure because my anxiety was creeping up. I started jogging lightly again in the spring, sometimes near the Queensboro Bridge when I am already in that area, and walking more in Cunningham Park. The senior center also asked me to help plan a monthly cooking workshop instead of just helping in the kitchen. That made me excited but also nervous, so now I spend Tuesday afternoons testing recipes and writing ingredient lists.

follow_ups.question: What recipe have you tested most recently?
follow_ups.response: A pork adobo with lemongrass and a side of roasted sweet potato with chili honey.

follow_ups.question: Has the new structure helped?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly. When I know what Tuesday is for, I don't drift into worry as much.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Nico wakes around 6:45, eats something quick like eggs or pandesal, and leaves for high school before 8. After school he has soccer in season, and other days he stays for homework help or comes home and plays video games after chores. I try to have dinner around 6:30 so he is not eating too late. Marielle's routine is more independent at college; she has classes, campus work-study sometimes, and she calls us Sunday evening.

follow_ups.question: How do you help Nico with school?
follow_ups.response: I check that assignments are done, but Lani helps more with writing. I help with projects where building or visuals are involved.

follow_ups.question: What does Nico do on weekends?
follow_ups.response: Soccer, cousins, games, and sometimes helping me in the yard if I push him.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Personally I have not had major trouble with law enforcement. Mostly traffic stops or seeing police around subway stations. But as an immigrant-looking Asian man with limited education, I learned early to be very polite and keep my hands visible, even if I did nothing wrong. That is just something in your body after years of hearing stories.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt treated unfairly by police?
follow_ups.response: Once during a traffic stop in the 2000s the officer talked to me like I was stupid because of my accent. It stayed with me.

follow_ups.question: Do you call police when there is a neighborhood problem?
follow_ups.response: For real danger, yes. For noise or small conflicts, neighbors usually talk first.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: After 9/11 there was a lot more police presence and people watching each other. My South Asian and Muslim neighbors seemed especially tense, and that affected how I understood policing.

follow_ups.question: Did that change your neighborhood relationships?
follow_ups.response: It made some people quieter, but on our block it also made neighbors check in more.

follow_ups.question: Any positive experiences?
follow_ups.response: A community officer once helped with a senior safety event, and that was useful and respectful.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. One cousin had a DUI years ago, but no one in my immediate family has had serious arrest problems.

follow_ups.question: How did the family respond to your cousin's DUI?
follow_ups.response: A lot of shame at first, then practical help. Rides, court dates, making sure it did not happen again.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you think about drinking and driving?
follow_ups.response: Yes. In our house, if anyone drinks, they are not driving. That is firm.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and most local elections now, but I was not always consistent when I was younger. I became more serious after becoming a citizen and after my kids got older and started asking questions. Lani reminds me about primary dates. I don't pretend I know every race, but I try to read enough to make a decent choice, especially for city council, schools, and health services.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide who to vote for?
follow_ups.response: I look at housing, health care, immigrant services, transit, and whether they seem connected to Queens.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote by mail or in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually in person. I like taking Nico with me so he sees the routine.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I lean Democratic, but I am not a loud party person. My politics come from family survival: affordable health care, fair wages, good public schools, safe streets without treating people like criminals, and respect for immigrants. I believe people should work hard, but I also know hard work alone does not solve rent, illness, language barriers, or a bad boss. I am more traditional about family than some younger people, maybe because of Catholic upbringing and Asian family culture, but I don't want government punishing people for being different. I care a lot about senior services because I see older Asian immigrants become invisible. So I am practical left-of-center, community-minded, and suspicious of politicians who only appear at festivals for photos.

follow_ups.question: What issues would make you change your vote?
follow_ups.response: Cuts to senior programs, anti-immigrant talk, or someone ignoring health care costs. Those are personal for me.

follow_ups.question: Do your family members agree politically?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, but my brother is more conservative about taxes and crime. We argue a little, then eat.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with Marielle. She pushes me to think about racism, climate, and gender more clearly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more open about mental health and public health as political issues. Before, I thought anxiety was just personal weakness, something to pray over or work through. Seeing seniors isolated during the pandemic and seeing my own anxiety get worse changed that. I also listen more to younger people about race and policing now. I still like practical solutions, but I understand better that systems can push people down quietly for years.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced that change most?
follow_ups.response: My daughter Marielle, and also seniors at the center who told stories about being ignored by hospitals or agencies.

follow_ups.question: Did the pandemic change your politics?
follow_ups.response: Yes. It made me see how much people depend on public systems when family alone is not enough.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat to a lot. I am not Black, so I don't pretend it is my same experience, but I recognize fear, being judged, and being talked down to. In Queens you live next to many histories, and you cannot say, 'That is not my problem.' The movement made me think about how Asian communities sometimes stay quiet because we want safety, but silence can also protect unfairness.

follow_ups.question: Did you discuss Black Lives Matter with your family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly at dinner in 2020 and 2021. Nico was younger, but Marielle had strong opinions and brought articles.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect how you see policing locally?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I still want safety, but I want accountability and better ways to handle mental health calls.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about dignity. If a person is already scared and then the system treats them as dangerous first, that does damage. I also think about how communities get divided: Asian store owners, Black customers, immigrant families, police, all carrying fear. For me the answer cannot be just slogans. It has to be training, accountability, jobs, youth programs, and neighbors actually knowing each other.

follow_ups.question: Do you support police reform?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially accountability, de-escalation, and mental health response teams.

follow_ups.question: Are there parts of the debate you struggle with?
follow_ups.response: When people talk like safety does not matter. Seniors in my community are scared too, so we need both justice and safety.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race in America is like something in the walls of an old house. You may not see it every second, but it shapes where the cracks appear. Anti-Asian hate during the pandemic shook me, especially older people being attacked. At the same time, I know Black Americans have carried a much longer and deeper burden here. I am trying to teach Nico that being proud of Filipino and Vietnamese roots should make him more aware of other people's struggles, not less.

follow_ups.question: Have you personally experienced anti-Asian bias?
follow_ups.response: Some comments, especially during COVID, like people muttering about China even though I am Filipino and Vietnamese. It made me angry and tired.

follow_ups.question: How do you respond when family makes racial comments?
follow_ups.response: I try to slow it down and ask what they mean. Sometimes elders repeat things from fear, but I still push back.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I mostly talked with family and friends. I did not join big protests because crowds make me anxious, but I donated a small amount once and attended a local community discussion.

follow_ups.question: What was the community discussion like?
follow_ups.response: It was at a church basement with neighbors from different backgrounds. People were honest but careful.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about these issues online?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. I may share a local event, but I don't like fighting on Facebook.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Marielle is the most vocal and progressive. Lani is quieter but cares deeply about safety for patients and elders. My brother Ramon is more law-and-order, especially after hearing about attacks on Asian seniors. My basketball friends are mixed; Luis talks about being stopped when he was younger, and Ahmed talks about post-9/11 suspicion. Those conversations made it more real than TV arguments.

follow_ups.question: Do these differences cause conflict?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but not permanent conflict. We usually come back to personal stories.

follow_ups.question: Whose view has challenged you most?
follow_ups.response: Luis, because he described police stops as a normal part of growing up, and that should not be normal.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am okay, but not perfect. I have lower back pain from years of maintenance work and some knee pain, especially after basketball. My doctor tells me to watch my blood pressure and weight. The bigger thing is anxiety. It comes as tight chest, racing thoughts, checking bills too many times, and eating snacks late when I cannot settle down.

follow_ups.question: Are you being treated for anxiety?
follow_ups.response: I talked to my primary doctor and had a few counseling sessions through a clinic. I am not on a daily medication right now.

follow_ups.question: What helps your body feel better?
follow_ups.response: Walking, stretching, gardening, lighter food, and not playing basketball like I am still twenty-five.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy is that I like cooking, so I can make vegetables taste good. Hard is portion control, late-night eating, and stress. Also, healthy food can get expensive if you are not careful. Exercise is easier in spring and fall, harder in winter when my mood drops.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually eat when stressed late at night?
follow_ups.response: Crackers, leftover rice, peanuts, sometimes ice cream. I know exactly where the problem is.

follow_ups.question: Do you plan meals for health or budget first?
follow_ups.response: Both. Beans, fish, greens, rice, soup, and whatever vegetables are on sale.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: No broken bones, but last year my back flared badly after I moved a cabinet for my sister. I was stuck walking like an old man for two weeks. My doctor also said my blood pressure was borderline high, so I started checking salt more carefully. Anxiety was the other big thing; one night I thought I was having a heart problem, but it turned out to be a panic attack.

follow_ups.question: What happened during the panic attack?
follow_ups.response: It was around 1 a.m., chest tight, sweating, thinking about bills and my mother's health. Lani almost took me to urgent care.

follow_ups.question: Did you follow up medically after that?
follow_ups.response: Yes, primary care checked me and suggested counseling, breathing exercises, and watching caffeine.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My back and anxiety are part of why I am not in regular paid work now. I can care for my family, but I pace myself and avoid heavy jobs.

follow_ups.question: What tasks are hardest physically?
follow_ups.response: Lifting appliances, crawling under sinks too long, and stairs with heavy laundry.

follow_ups.question: Does anxiety interrupt caregiving?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I overcheck things or get irritable, then I have to apologize and reset.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, my mother's health is a constant concern. She has diabetes and arthritis, and she gets lonely even living with my sister. Lani's work also exposes her to patients who are sick, so during COVID we were very careful. I do rides, pharmacy pickups, and food for my mother because food is how I can care without making her feel helpless.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help your mother with health needs?
follow_ups.response: At least twice a week in person and phone calls every morning.

follow_ups.question: Does caregiving affect your stress?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I love her, but medical appointments and insurance papers make my chest tight.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have managed, but it takes work. Lani gets insurance through her job, but copays and dental costs still hurt. I have delayed dental work because it felt too expensive. For mental health, finding someone affordable and culturally comfortable was hard. My mother needs translation sometimes, and if I or my sister do not go, things get missed.

follow_ups.question: What care have you postponed?
follow_ups.response: Dental cleaning and a crown evaluation. I kept saying next month.

follow_ups.question: What makes a provider feel trustworthy?
follow_ups.response: They listen, don't rush accents, explain costs, and understand family caregiving.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, in our family we use home remedies along with regular doctors. Ginger tea, turmeric, steam, menthol rub, Vietnamese herbal soups, and sometimes coin rubbing when older relatives insist. My mother believes in certain bitter teas for blood sugar, though we remind her not to replace medicine. I use breathing, prayer, gardening, and cooking as informal medicine for my nerves.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those remedies?

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: In New York she did sewing alterations and later kitchen prep work. She hemmed pants, repaired clothes, chopped vegetables, washed dishes, and helped prepare trays of food. Her important duties were speed, neatness, and not wasting anything.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked in small garment shops and later restaurant kitchens and catering places in Queens. The garment shops altered clothing, and the kitchens prepared takeout, party trays, and everyday meals. They were small immigrant businesses, not big companies.

follow_ups.response: Not very. Hours changed and pay was modest.

transcript.response: Yes, my dad worked for pay for many years.

follow_ups.question: Did you work with him?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially after we came to New York.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad did building maintenance, painting, repairs, and janitorial work. He fixed leaks, patched walls, cleaned halls, moved supplies, and dealt with tenants or supervisors. His most important duty was being dependable and willing to take hard jobs.

follow_ups.question: What did he teach you directly?
follow_ups.response: Measure twice, shut off water first, and never leave a customer with a bigger mess.

follow_ups.question: Did he like the work?
follow_ups.response: He liked being useful, but it wore him down.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for small property owners, apartment buildings, and maintenance contractors. They provided housing repairs, cleaning, and basic building upkeep. It was practical work: keep the heat on, keep water running, keep tenants from calling twice.

follow_ups.question: Was he self-employed?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes he took side jobs, but mostly he worked for small employers.

follow_ups.question: Did his work influence your path?
follow_ups.response: Completely. My hands learned from his hands.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope the cooking workshop is real and steady, maybe with a small stipend, maybe connected to a community health outreach certificate. I want to teach Filipino and Vietnamese recipes to seniors and younger people together, but also use the meal as a way to talk about loneliness, anxiety, and taking care of each other. I hope Nico is doing well after high school and Marielle finishes college without too much debt. I hope Lani can work less hard. For myself, I want my body to be stronger, my anxiety quieter, and maybe I want to learn watercolor so I can paint the same Queens streets I photograph.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward the workshop?
follow_ups.response: Writing a simple proposal for the senior center director with budget, recipes, and health themes.

follow_ups.question: What would success feel like?
follow_ups.response: A room of elders eating, laughing, taking leftovers home, and someone saying they felt less alone.

follow_ups.question: Where would you like to travel next if money allowed?
follow_ups.response: Maybe Vietnam with Lani, or back to Kyoto to learn more about tea and careful cooking.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family, dignity, and usefulness. I value feeding people because food carries memory and care without needing perfect English. I value keeping promises, paying attention to elders, and staying curious even when life is tight. I also value beauty in ordinary places: steam from soup, light on a subway platform, a good jazz record, a tomato from the backyard. Those things keep me human.

follow_ups.question: What value do you hope your children learn from you?
follow_ups.response: Respect people who work hard in quiet jobs, and don't be ashamed of where your family started.

follow_ups.question: What do you want people to remember about you?
follow_ups.response: That I showed up, cooked enough for everyone, and fixed what I could.
